_comment: Per-request work that is unbounded BY CONSTRUCTION and that
scripts/check_perf_regressions.py has seen and ACCEPTED, each with the
reason. The checker fails on any finding not listed here, and equally on any
entry here that no longer matches a finding -- a stale allowance is how a ban
quietly stops applying, and it is the direction a 'what's new' reader never
thinks to check.
WHY THIS LEDGER IS EMPTY, which is the intended steady state rather than a
gap. The measured baseline was 70 request-body consumption sites against 0
outer ceilings: 68 `json.NewDecoder(r.Body)` and 2 bare `io.ReadAll(r.Body)`,
with `http.MaxBytesReader` appearing nowhere in the tree. Recording 70
accepted entries would have produced a ledger that DOCUMENTS the problem
instead of closing it, so the same change landed the repair instead:
* ONE outer bound at the root handler (internal/server.Server.boundBodies),
which is the only ceiling the 68 decoder sites ever needed -- a streaming
decoder allocates as it reads, and one bound at the root closes the class
rather than the 68 instances. Behind FABRIC_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES with a
320 MiB default and 0 meaning unlimited, because it NARROWS what a
released binary accepts and no such narrowing may ship unremarked.
* BOTH bare reads moved onto httpx.ReadBounded
(internal/onelake/principalaccess.go, internal/api/dataaccessmode.go).
Neither was covered by internal/httpx/guard_test.go, which bans the
`io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(...))` idiom -- a bound that truncates --
and is blind to the absence of a bound altogether.
So all four kinds ship at zero entries. `unbounded-body-read` is empty
because it was repaired; `missing-outer-bound` and
`ceiling-above-outer-bound` are assertions that the repair still holds and
should never gain an entry at all; `recompiled-regexp` is empty because all 9
regexp sites are package-level today, and is defined so a future per-call
compile lands as a recorded decision rather than an unnoticed cost -- the same
precedent `long-sleep` set in docs/vitest-test-flakiness.json.
The OneLake data plane needs no exemption here, which is worth stating
because an earlier design gave it one. The outer bound sits ABOVE
httpx.MaxBlobWrite (320 MiB against 256 MiB), so large Delta and Parquet
uploads are untouched and still fail -- when they do -- with httpx's own
fit-vs-truncated message rather than a generic refusal. Excluding the data
plane would have left the surface most able to exhaust memory as the one
surface with no ceiling.
See docs/62-performance-regressions.md for the full sweep, including the
loop-shaped heuristics that were measured and deliberately rejected.
